children.text: What you just heard was the opening selection of “St. Louis Blues,” performed by Louis Armstrong (with Velma Middleton & his All Stars) in 1954. Quickly becoming a jazz standard, it tells the story of a woman mourning her absent lover. Even without vocals, the mournful cornet, tinkling piano, and forlorn trombone join together to convey a story about loss – in fact, it’s very likely you wrote down something about how the recording sounds sad, all without knowing anything about the specifics of the story. Did you notice how that feeling was created? With what sounds, beats, rhythms, or tones?

Sound is evocative, conjuring feelings and memories that resonate deeply with listeners. For poets, sound can be one of the most powerful tools for expressing personal experiences and connecting those experiences to something larger—their communities, cultures, or sense of place. Yet, we often forget to listen for sound in poetry because we’re so focused on breaking down the words on the page and “solving” for the “right answer.”
Today, we’ll slow down and listen to what poetry can reveal when we pay attention not only to what a poet says, but how their words sound. Let’s start by exploring a poem by Langston Hughes!

, Langston Hughes (1901-1967) was a central figure in the Harlem Renaissance. The Harlem Renaissance – much like the European Renaissance – referred to an explosion of art and ideas. This explosion was centered in Harlem, New York City, and specifically defined a period of creation from Black artists in early 20th century America, in which these artists celebrated their identities and rejected racial discrimination in their works. A pioneer of jazz poetry, Hughes worked to portray an honest depiction of working-class Black lives, often by embracing the musical structures found in jazz or blues poetry. Remember our opening song? “St. Louis Blues” was actually one of Hughes’s favorite jazz poems,
Keep in mind this contextual information as you listen to Hughes perform his 1951 poem, “Harlem (A Dream Deferred).” Be sure that as you read, you also annotate for things that stick out to you.
